title: Velocity AI - Redwood discovery: migration OpenAI -> Dedicated/Private
next_steps: Redwood to share Dedicated pricing and pilot SOW by 2026-03-04
SE to propose benchmark plan and load test template by 2026-03-05
Customer to provide ~100 sample prompts and recent traffic profile by 2026-03-03
action_items: Maya: send pricing, seat/license options, and draft SOW by 2026-03-04
Liam: run initial benchmark spec and share load test template by 2026-03-05
Ian: upload sample prompt set and 3 anonymized logs for seq len distribution by 2026-03-03

summary: Velocity AI is evaluating migration from OpenAI-hosted endpoints to Redwood Dedicated or a Private deployment. Main drivers: predictable latency, unit cost savings at scale, and data residency/compliance. Key risks: eval parity with current OpenAI models, compatibility with their vLLM-based stack (TGI experiments), and SSO/KMS integration. Agreement to run a POC with benchmarks and share prompts and traffic profile.
transcript:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. I'm Maya from Redwood, account exec. with me is Liam our solutions engineer. how's everyone doing?
[00:06] Sofia: Doing good, thanks. Sofia here, CTO at Velocity. We have Ian our ML lead, Raj from security, and Tracy PM.
[00:12] Maya: Awesome. Quick agenda: understand current infra, drivers for migration, must-haves, and agree next steps. Sound good?
[00:18] Tracy: Yep.
[00:20] Ian: Yep.
[00:22] Liam: Great, I'll jump in on the technical bits as we go.
[00:26] Sofia: Cool, starting with context: we've been on OpenAI hosted for two years. Most prod traffic hits gpt-4-ish endpoints for chat and generation, and we also run some on-prem experiments using vLLM and TGI for cost-sensitive batch jobs. Primary concerns are latency spikes, token costs at scale, and enterprise compliance for some EU customers.
[00:42] Maya: Got it. When you say latency spikes, can you quantify typical p95 or p99?
[00:46] Ian: p95 for chat flows is around 650 to 900ms depending on peak time, p99 can go to 1.6-1.8s which for our interactive use is noticeable. batch jobs are fine but the cost per 1M tokens is becoming an issue.
[01:01] Sofia: Also want to avoid vendor lock-in. We ran a couple tests with vLLM to see if self-hosting lowers cost, but ops burden is heavy.
[01:10] Liam: Makes sense. On the Dedicated side we offer reserved GPU pools that can give you very predictable p95s under SLOs, plus autoscaling for bursts. For Private we can do VPC or on-prem with a customer-controlled control plane if you have strict residency needs.
[01:26] Raj: From security side, we need SOC2 and control over KMS/HSM and audit logs. Do you support SAML/SSO and per-route audit?
[01:33] Maya: Yes, we have SOC2 compliance and can integrate with customer KMS via standard KMIP or cloud KMS. SSO/SAML OK, and Console has per-route logs and token-level cost breakdown. We'll share the compliance pack.
[01:45] Raj: Great.
[01:47] Ian: A big technical question: our stack is vLLM-based for local inference and TGI experiments. How compatible is Redwood runtime with our current prompt templates and tokenization? We rely on some custom system prompts and a KV cache pattern.
[02:00] Liam: Good question. Redwood's runtime supports standard tokenizer families but there are subtle differences across model variants. For the most part prompt templates should be drop-in, but we recommend running a parity eval because of differences in model weights and decoding defaults. KV cache support is supported in Dedicated/Private with efficient cache warming and prefix caching to avoid repeated compute.
[02:20] Ian: Can we bring our own model weights? We are exploring an open model + quantization route.
[02:24] Liam: On Private deployments, yes, you can host your own model artifacts and we have guidance for quantized runtimes. For Hosted and Dedicated we offer curated model catalog; Dedicated can host customer model bundles if needed under the Dedicated contract. There's also model pinning and rollout controls.
[02:40] Sofia: Eval parity is crucial — we can't accept regressions. How do you validate parity?
[02:44] Maya: We do eval sets and can run A/B tests during the POC. Our Optimize team suggests quantization profiles and provides quality monitoring with regression alerts tied to a prompt set. For contractual POCs we can run side-by-side tests using your prompts and metric set (BLEU/ROUGE/task-specific metrics).
[03:00] Ian: Ok. We also use function calling patterns in a couple of flows. Any limitations there?
[03:04] Liam: We support structured outputs and function-calling style APIs. On Dedicated/Private you'll have full parity, but if you run custom model artifacts we might need minor adapter work for some custom tooling — we'll scope that in the POC.
[03:18] Tracy: On pricing, what's the expected delta vs OpenAI per token? At our scale we need to look at 100s of millions of tokens a month.
[03:26] Maya: Pricing depends on deployment. Hosted is similar to market; Dedicated offers committed capacity pricing which often reduces unit cost significantly at scale due to reserved GPU economics. Private has platform fees plus infra. We'll send a modeled cost comparison with your traffic profile.
[03:38] Sofia: When you say Dedicated, is that single-tenant GPUs or multi-tenant VMs? We need data isolation.
[03:44] Liam: Dedicated is reserved GPU pools logically isolated to your tenancy. Not multi-tenant noisy neighbors. You get guaranteed throughput and isolation at the infra layer.
[03:52] Raj: Data retention and logs — will logs ever leave our VPC? For Private we want full control.
[03:58] Maya: For Private VPC/on-prem, control plane can be customer-managed and logs stay in your environment. For Dedicated we provide retention settings and can restrict telemetry, and we support DPA terms for data handling. We'll include the options in the compliance pack.
[04:12] Ian: A more niche thing — we heavily use KV caching to accelerate long-chat sessions. How does Redwood handle KV and cache eviction?
[04:19] Liam: We have a runtime that supports efficient KV cache management, automatic prefix cache warming, and configurable cache eviction policies. We also have batching-aware cache that avoids duplicative compute for similar prefixes. We'll include a tech note on cache behavior.
[04:33] Sofia: Great. Another question: compatibility with our current orchestration and routing — we use a mixture of Kubernetes and an internal router that shards by tenant. Can Redwood integrate into that with routing policies?
[04:44] Liam: Yes, smart routing is supported. You can route by policy (latency, cost, region, customer tier). For Dedicated we'll provide endpoints compatible with your internal orchestrator and can support canary rollouts, A/B tests, and automatic fallback.
[04:58] Ian: About benchmarks — what do you need from us to run a realistic benchmark?
[05:02] Liam: Ideally: a sample prompt set representative of your top 1000 prompts, payload sizes and sequence length distribution, concurrency profile (RPS), and the quality metric thresholds you use. We'll run side-by-side with similar model variants and provide latency percentiles, cost per token, and throughput curves.
[05:22] Tracy: Any gotchas if we tried to port everything to Dedicated but keep some cross-over with OpenAI for edge cases?
[05:28] Maya: You can run hybrid routing — route most traffic to Dedicated and fall back to hosted OpenAI or Redwood-hosted model variants for unexpected capacity. Fallback policies are supported.
[05:37] Sofia: Security question: do you allow bringing our own KMS so keys never transit Redwood?
[05:41] Maya: For Private yes; for Dedicated we support customer KMS integrations per contract so keys can be managed in your cloud KMS. We'll clarify the exact flow in the compliance docs.
[05:52] Raj: Encryption in transit and at rest — confirm AES-256 at rest and TLS 1.2+ in transit?
[05:57] Liam: Yes on TLS 1.2+ and AES-256 for storage, plus disk-level encryption on Private.
[06:04] Ian: One more operational question: how do you handle model upgrades and rollouts without causing user-visible regressions?
[06:10] Liam: We provide model pinning, gradual canaries, automatic fallback to previous model variants, and an evaluation monitor that triggers alerts on quality drift against your test set. You can schedule rollouts and set automatic rollback thresholds.
[06:25] Sofia: Ok, seems promising. On timelines: we want to run a POC in mid-March. Is that feasible?
[06:30] Maya: Yes, that's feasible. Typical POC timeline is 2-4 weeks for a focused pilot: baseline tests, side-by-side parity evals, and a production-like load test. We'll need your prompts and traffic profile to scope infra.
[06:42] Tracy: For billing during POC — trial credits?
[06:45] Maya: We usually provide POC credits and discounted Dedicated trial pricing; specifics we'll put in the SOW.
[06:52] Ian: We also experiment with packaging models into quantized artifacts using 4-bit/8-bit; any recommended quantization profiles?
[06:58] Liam: Our Optimize team recommends model- and workload-specific quantization profiles. For many LLMs 4-bit quantization with proper calibration keeps quality near baseline. We'll include guidance and past benchmarks.
[07:12] Sofia: Are there customers in our industry who have migrated? Any references?
[07:16] Maya: Yes, we have a couple in fintech and a health customer who moved to Dedicated for residency needs — we can share anonymized references and a case study.
[07:26] Raj: One operational detail — do you provide per-token cost breakdowns and route-level billing? We need chargeback for internal cost allocation.
[07:32] Liam: Console provides token-level cost and per-route model dashboards; you can export cost per route for internal billing.
[07:40] Maya: Ok great, let's recap real quick. Action items: Maya will send pricing and draft SOW; Liam will prepare benchmark plan and load test template; Velocity to provide sample prompts, sequence-length distribution, and RPS profile; Raj to share compliance contact. We'll aim to kick off POC week of March 8.
[07:58] Sofia: That works. Anything else from Redwood?
[08:01] Liam: I'll add a short tech note on KV cache and quantization edge cases.
[08:05] Maya: We'll also include the compliance pack and some reference case studies.
[08:09] Tracy: Thanks all.
[08:11] Sofia: Thanks, bye.
[08:12] Maya: Thanks everyone, talk soon. Bye.

Notes on transcript quality: occasional words mis-transcribed (e.g., gpt-4-ish heard as gpt four ish), speaker labels inferred by system, timestamps approx every 15-60s. Some technical terms abbreviated or slightly off (vLLM sometimes transcribed as v-l-l-m), natural crosstalk present.
